Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Which of the following best defines economics as a social science?
options: The study of how government controls prices of goods
The study of how society allocates scarce resources to satisfy unlimited human wants
The study of how money is printed and circulated
The study of how firms advertise their products
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: The study of how society allocates scarce resources to satisfy unlimited human wants

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: The fundamental economic problem that gives rise to the need for choice is:
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Scarcity

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Scarcity in economics refers to a situation where:
options: Goods are completely unavailable in the market
Prices of goods are too high for consumers
Resources are limited relative to the unlimited wants they can satisfy
The government has banned the production of a good
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Resources are limited relative to the unlimited wants they can satisfy

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Choice becomes necessary in economics mainly because:
options: Resources are scarce while human wants are unlimited
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Resources are scarce while human wants are unlimited

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: A scale of preference is best described as:
options: A list of a consumer's income sources
A ranking of wants in order of importance or urgency
A government policy on price control
A record of a firm's total output
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: A ranking of wants in order of importance or urgency

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: The main purpose of drawing up a scale of preference is to help an individual:
options: Decide which wants to satisfy first with limited resources
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Decide which wants to satisfy first with limited resources

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Opportunity cost is best defined as:
options: The total cost of producing a good
The amount of money paid for a good
The value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made
The cost of transporting goods to the market
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: The value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Opportunity cost is also commonly referred to as:
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Alternative or forgone cost

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: A student has GH₵200 and can either buy textbooks or a pair of shoes, both costing GH₵200. If she buys the textbooks, the opportunity cost is:
options: Nothing, since she made a wise choice
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: The pair of shoes forgone

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: The production possibility curve (PPC) shows:
options: The maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with given resources and technology
The trend of prices of two goods over time
The exchange rate between two currencies
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: The maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with given resources and technology

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: The production possibility curve is typically drawn concave to the origin because of:
options: Increasing opportunity cost as more of one good is produced
Falling prices of factors of production
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Increasing opportunity cost as more of one good is produced

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: A point lying exactly on the production possibility curve represents:
options: Full and efficient use of available resources
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Full and efficient use of available resources

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: A point lying inside the production possibility curve indicates that:
options: Resources are fully and efficiently utilised
The economy has achieved maximum growth
The combination of goods is impossible to produce
Resources are underutilised or inefficiently used
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Resources are underutilised or inefficiently used

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: A point lying outside the production possibility curve is described as:
options: Unattainable with the current level of resources and technology
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Unattainable with the current level of resources and technology

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: An outward shift of the entire production possibility curve is most likely caused by:
options: An increase in resources or improvement in technology
A decrease in the labour force
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: An increase in resources or improvement in technology

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: In economics, production refers to:
options: The buying of goods for personal use
The sharing of income among factors of production
The creation of goods and services to satisfy human wants
The storage of finished goods in warehouses
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: The creation of goods and services to satisfy human wants

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Distribution, as an economic activity, mainly refers to:
options: The manufacturing of raw materials into finished goods
The direct use of goods to satisfy wants
The extraction of raw materials from nature
The movement of goods and services from producers to final consumers
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: The movement of goods and services from producers to final consumers

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Consumption in economics is best described as:
options: The process of growing crops for sale
The transportation of goods from farm to market
The final use of goods and services to satisfy human wants
The process of assembling raw materials into finished products
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: The final use of goods and services to satisfy human wants

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Which of the following economic activities is classified under the primary sector?
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Fishing

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: The secondary sector of the economy is chiefly concerned with:
options: The extraction of raw materials directly from nature
The provision of services such as education and health
The processing and manufacturing of raw materials into finished goods
The wholesale and retail distribution of goods
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: The processing and manufacturing of raw materials into finished goods

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Which of the following best represents an activity in the tertiary sector?
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Banking and insurance services

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: The primary sector contributes to the economy mainly by:
options: Providing raw materials and food for the population and industries
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Providing raw materials and food for the population and industries

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: One major contribution of the tertiary sector to a country's economy is:
options: Direct extraction of minerals from the earth
Provision of essential services such as education, health, and finance that support other sectors
Cultivation of cash crops for export
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Provision of essential services such as education, health, and finance that support other sectors

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: The three basic economic problems faced by every society are:
options: What to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: What to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Human wants, as studied in economics, are best described as:
options: Equal in intensity for all individuals
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Unlimited and recurring

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: A good that is scarce and commands a price because resources are used to produce it is known as:
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: An economic good

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: A free good differs from an economic good in that a free good:
options: Must always be purchased with money
Is always produced by the government
Is scarce and requires factors of production
Has no opportunity cost because it exists in unlimited supply relative to demand
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Has no opportunity cost because it exists in unlimited supply relative to demand

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes scarcity from poverty?
options: Scarcity only affects poor countries while poverty affects rich countries
Scarcity is a universal economic condition affecting all societies, while poverty refers to a lack of adequate resources to meet basic needs
Poverty and scarcity mean exactly the same thing
Scarcity can be completely eliminated by government policy, but poverty cannot
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Scarcity is a universal economic condition affecting all societies, while poverty refers to a lack of adequate resources to meet basic needs

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: A trader ranks her wants as: rent (1st), food (2nd), school fees (3rd), new clothes (4th). If she has enough money to satisfy only her top two wants, this ranking illustrates:
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: A scale of preference

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: A farmer with one plot of land can plant either 100 bags of maize or 60 bags of yam. If he decides to plant maize alone, the opportunity cost is:
options: Zero, since he chose the better option
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: 60 bags of yam forgone

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: On a production possibility curve for guns and butter, moving along the curve from more butter to more guns illustrates:
options: A trade-off, since producing more guns means producing less butter
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: A trade-off, since producing more guns means producing less butter

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Which of the following is NOT generally regarded as a cause of scarcity?
options: Limited technology at a point in time
Abundant supply of every resource needed by man
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Abundant supply of every resource needed by man

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Vehicle assembly plants and textile mills belong to which sector of the economy?
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Secondary sector

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Crop farming, livestock rearing, and mining are all examples of activities in the:
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Primary sector

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Which of the following best describes the scope of economics as a discipline?
options: It studies how individuals, firms, and governments make choices in allocating scarce resources among competing uses
It studies only how governments raise taxes
It studies only the buying and selling of shares
It studies only the history of money
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: It studies how individuals, firms, and governments make choices in allocating scarce resources among competing uses

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: The branch of economics that studies individual units such as households and firms is called:
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Microeconomics

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: "The cost of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made" is the definition of:
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Opportunity cost

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: For an economy to move from a point inside its production possibility curve to a point on the curve, it must:
options: Fully utilise its existing idle resources more efficiently
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Fully utilise its existing idle resources more efficiently

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: Which of the following correctly orders the stages of economic activity that a loaf of bread passes through before it is eaten?
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Production, distribution, consumption

Definition and Scope of Economics.text: A senior secondary school leaver decides to study Economics instead of Government at university, even though he cannot study both. The best subject he gives up is called the:
Definition and Scope of Economics.correct_answer: Opportunity cost of studying Economics

Factors of Production.text: In economics, land as a factor of production refers to:
options: Only the soil used for farming
Buildings and machinery used in production
All natural resources provided by nature, such as soil, water, minerals, and forests
Factors of Production.correct_answer: All natural resources provided by nature, such as soil, water, minerals, and forests

Factors of Production.text: Which of the following is a distinguishing characteristic of land as a factor of production?
options: It can be easily reproduced when demand increases
Its total supply is fixed and cannot be increased by man
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Its total supply is fixed and cannot be increased by man

Factors of Production.text: The reward paid to the owner of land for its use in production is called:
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Rent

Factors of Production.text: Labour, as a factor of production, is best defined as:
options: Any human effort, physical or mental, directed towards the production of goods and services
The machinery used in a factory
The natural resources used in farming
The money used to start a business
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Any human effort, physical or mental, directed towards the production of goods and services

Factors of Production.text: Which of the following is a peculiar characteristic of labour as a factor of production?
options: It is inseparable from the labourer providing it
It can be stored indefinitely for future use
It is a gift of nature
Factors of Production.correct_answer: It is inseparable from the labourer providing it

Factors of Production.text: The reward for labour in production is known as:
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Wage or salary

Factors of Production.text: A surgeon and a bricklayer both provide labour, but the surgeon requires years of specialised training. The surgeon's labour is best classified as:
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Skilled labour

Factors of Production.text: Division of labour refers to:
options: The breaking down of a production process into separate tasks performed by different workers
The equal sharing of profit among workers
The distribution of land among farmers
The payment of different wages to workers
Factors of Production.correct_answer: The breaking down of a production process into separate tasks performed by different workers

Factors of Production.text: Which of the following is an advantage of division of labour?
options: It increases efficiency and output through specialisation
It leads to greater dependence on other producers
It reduces the total output of an economy
Factors of Production.correct_answer: It increases efficiency and output through specialisation

Factors of Production.text: A major disadvantage of division of labour is that it can lead to:
options: Faster acquisition of varied skills by each worker
Monotony and loss of job satisfaction among workers
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Monotony and loss of job satisfaction among workers

Factors of Production.text: Capital, as a factor of production, refers to:
options: Natural resources such as land and minerals
Man-made resources such as machinery, tools, and buildings used to produce other goods and services
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Man-made resources such as machinery, tools, and buildings used to produce other goods and services

Factors of Production.text: Fixed capital differs from circulating capital in that fixed capital:
options: Is used up completely in a single production process
Refers only to cash held by a firm
Can be used repeatedly over a long period, such as machinery and buildings
Cannot be owned by private individuals
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Can be used repeatedly over a long period, such as machinery and buildings

Factors of Production.text: Which of the following best exemplifies circulating (working) capital?
options: Raw materials and stocks awaiting processing or sale
A delivery truck used for ten years
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Raw materials and stocks awaiting processing or sale

Factors of Production.text: A key characteristic that distinguishes capital from land is that capital:
options: Is man-made and results from past savings and investment
Is entirely a gift of nature
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Is man-made and results from past savings and investment

Factors of Production.text: The reward for the use of capital in production is called:
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Interest

Factors of Production.text: An entrepreneur is best described as the person who:
options: Provides physical labour on a farm
Lends money to businesses at interest
Organises the other factors of production and bears the risk of business
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Organises the other factors of production and bears the risk of business

Factors of Production.text: Which of the following is a major function of the entrepreneur?
options: Bearing the risks and uncertainties of business
Fixing the market price of land
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Bearing the risks and uncertainties of business

Factors of Production.text: The reward for entrepreneurship is:
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Profit

Factors of Production.text: An important characteristic of a successful entrepreneur is:
options: Reluctance to combine factors of production
Dependence on government for daily business decisions
Innovativeness and the ability to identify new business opportunities
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Innovativeness and the ability to identify new business opportunities

Factors of Production.text: Which factor of production is commonly referred to as a "gift of nature"?
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Land

Factors of Production.text: Which factor of production is generally regarded as the risk-bearing and organising factor?
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Entrepreneurship

Factors of Production.text: Geographical mobility of labour refers to the ability of a worker to:
options: Move from one location to another in search of work
Move from one occupation to another within the same location
Change from skilled to unskilled work
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Move from one location to another in search of work

Factors of Production.text: Occupational mobility of labour refers to the ability of a worker to:
options: Change from one type of job or occupation to another
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Change from one type of job or occupation to another

Factors of Production.text: Which of the following factors would most likely increase the efficiency of labour?
options: Poor health and inadequate feeding of workers
Adequate training, good health, and motivation of workers
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Adequate training, good health, and motivation of workers

Factors of Production.text: Capital formation refers to:
options: The act of spending all income on consumption
The distribution of wages to workers
The process of adding to a nation's stock of capital goods through saving and investment
The extraction of raw materials from land
Factors of Production.correct_answer: The process of adding to a nation's stock of capital goods through saving and investment

Factors of Production.text: Which of the following is an example of fixed capital?
options: Raw cotton in a textile mill awaiting processing
Unsold finished goods in a warehouse
A factory machine used for several years
Factors of Production.correct_answer: A factory machine used for several years

Factors of Production.text: One key difference between land and labour as factors of production is that:
options: Labour is a gift of nature while land is man-made
Land can get tired while labour cannot
Labour has a completely fixed supply while land does not
Land is a passive factor while labour is an active, human factor
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Land is a passive factor while labour is an active, human factor

Factors of Production.text: Unlike labour, entrepreneurship is distinguished mainly by its role in:
options: Coordinating land, labour, and capital while bearing business risk
Supplying only physical strength to production
Receiving a fixed wage regardless of business performance
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Coordinating land, labour, and capital while bearing business risk

Factors of Production.text: "Real capital" refers to:
options: Money kept in a savings account
Shares and bonds traded on the stock exchange
Physical assets such as machines, tools, and buildings used in production
Cash used to pay workers' wages
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Physical assets such as machines, tools, and buildings used in production

Factors of Production.text: The importance of land to an economy includes all of the following EXCEPT that it:
options: Provides space for agriculture and construction
Can be increased in total quantity through manufacturing
Supplies raw materials such as minerals and timber
Serves as a site for economic activities
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Can be increased in total quantity through manufacturing

Factors of Production.text: The entrepreneur is important to production mainly because he/she:
options: Supplies only the natural resources needed
Combines land, labour, and capital efficiently to produce goods and services
Receives a fixed wage for services rendered
Is exempted from bearing any business risk
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Combines land, labour, and capital efficiently to produce goods and services

Factors of Production.text: Wages may differ between two workers in the same country mainly due to differences in:
options: Skill, experience, qualification, and nature of the job
The season of the year only
The size of the country's population
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Skill, experience, qualification, and nature of the job

Factors of Production.text: Interest, as the reward for capital, is best described as the payment for:
options: The use of borrowed capital or the postponement of present consumption (waiting)
Bearing the risk of running a business
Factors of Production.correct_answer: The use of borrowed capital or the postponement of present consumption (waiting)

Factors of Production.text: Economic rent, in the classical (Ricardian) sense, refers to:
options: The wage paid to agricultural labourers
The interest earned on money invested in land
The total profit made by a farmer
A payment made for the use of land in excess of what is required to keep it in its present use
Factors of Production.correct_answer: A payment made for the use of land in excess of what is required to keep it in its present use

Factors of Production.text: Profit is often described as a residual income because it:
options: Is paid before all other factor rewards are settled
Is fixed regardless of business performance
Is the amount remaining after all other costs of production, including rent, wages, and interest, have been paid
Is guaranteed by government to every entrepreneur
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Is the amount remaining after all other costs of production, including rent, wages, and interest, have been paid

Factors of Production.text: Compared to land, capital and labour are generally considered:
options: More mobile and can be increased or redirected between uses
Fixed in total supply like land
Factors of Production.correct_answer: More mobile and can be increased or redirected between uses

Factors of Production.text: Human capital refers to:
options: The money a firm borrows from a bank
The skills, knowledge, and training embodied in workers that improve their productivity
The natural resources found on a piece of land
Factors of Production.correct_answer: The skills, knowledge, and training embodied in workers that improve their productivity

Factors of Production.text: The supply of labour in an economy is most directly influenced by:
options: Population size, wage levels, and working conditions
The total land area of the country
The interest rate on government bonds only
The amount of rent charged on farmland
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Population size, wage levels, and working conditions

Factors of Production.text: Mrs. Adjei owns a bakery. She rents the shop building, pays her workers monthly salaries, borrowed money from a bank to buy an oven, and personally organises production while bearing the risk of loss. The reward she personally earns as the organiser of the business is called:
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Profit

Factors of Production.text: A farm has fertile soil (a), a tractor (b), farm workers (c), and a manager who plans and takes business risks (d). Which pair correctly matches a factor of production with its reward?
Factors of Production.correct_answer: Farm workers (labour) — wage

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: An economic system may be defined as:
options: A method of printing currency notes
A list of taxes imposed by government
The way a society organises itself to solve the basic economic problems of what, how, and for whom to produce
A record of a country's exports and imports
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: The way a society organises itself to solve the basic economic problems of what, how, and for whom to produce

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: Capitalism, also known as the free enterprise or market economic system, is best defined as a system in which:
options: The government owns and controls all means of production
Means of production are privately owned and economic decisions are guided mainly by market forces
Land is owned communally by the whole village
All prices are fixed by a central planning authority
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Means of production are privately owned and economic decisions are guided mainly by market forces

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: A key feature of a capitalist economic system is:
options: Freedom of private individuals to own property and undertake business for profit
State ownership of all factors of production
Complete elimination of the profit motive
A total ban on private enterprise
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Freedom of private individuals to own property and undertake business for profit

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: In a capitalist economy, the question of "what to produce" is primarily determined by:
options: The forces of demand and supply operating through the price mechanism
A central planning committee appointed by government
Traditional customs handed down through generations
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: The forces of demand and supply operating through the price mechanism

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: One major advantage of the capitalist economic system is that it:
options: Guarantees equal distribution of income among all citizens
Encourages efficiency and innovation through competition and the profit motive
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Encourages efficiency and innovation through competition and the profit motive

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: A major disadvantage commonly associated with the capitalist economic system is:
options: Lack of incentive for entrepreneurs to innovate
Wide inequality in the distribution of income and wealth
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Wide inequality in the distribution of income and wealth

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: Socialism, as an economic system, is best described as one in which:
options: Private individuals freely own all factors of production
The means of production are collectively or state owned and economic activity is centrally planned
Prices are determined solely by private competition
Government has no role in the economy whatsoever
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: The means of production are collectively or state owned and economic activity is centrally planned

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: A distinguishing feature of a socialist economic system is:
options: Reliance on the free interplay of market forces to allocate resources
Complete absence of any government planning
State or collective ownership of the major means of production
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: State or collective ownership of the major means of production

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: In a socialist economy, the basic economic problems are mainly resolved through:
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Central planning by the state

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: One advantage of a socialist economic system is that it tends to:
options: Promote a more equitable distribution of income and resources among citizens
Encourage cut-throat competition among private firms
Rely entirely on the profit motive to allocate resources
Eliminate the need for any economic planning
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Promote a more equitable distribution of income and resources among citizens

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: A major disadvantage of the socialist economic system is:
options: Uncontrolled monopoly power by private firms
Total absence of government involvement in production
Lack of individual incentive and initiative, which can lead to inefficiency
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Lack of individual incentive and initiative, which can lead to inefficiency

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: A mixed economic system is best defined as one in which:
options: Only the government owns and controls all resources
Only private individuals own and control all resources
Barter is the only means of exchange
Both the public (government) sector and the private sector co-exist and jointly participate in economic activity
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Both the public (government) sector and the private sector co-exist and jointly participate in economic activity

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: Which of the following is a key feature of a mixed economy?
options: Complete state ownership of all industries
Total absence of private property rights
Prices fixed exclusively by traditional custom
A combination of market forces and government intervention in solving economic problems
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: A combination of market forces and government intervention in solving economic problems

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: One advantage of a mixed economic system is that it:
options: Completely removes the government from economic activities
Guarantees that no monopoly can ever exist
Combines the efficiency of private enterprise with government intervention to reduce inequality and correct market failures
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Combines the efficiency of private enterprise with government intervention to reduce inequality and correct market failures

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: A possible disadvantage of a mixed economic system is:
options: It always leads to complete state ownership of resources
It can lead to conflict between public and private sector goals and result in bureaucratic delays
It cannot allow for any private business activity
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: It can lead to conflict between public and private sector goals and result in bureaucratic delays

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: Which of the following countries is most often cited as a classic historical example of a centrally planned socialist economy?
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: The former Soviet Union

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: The basic economic problem of "what to produce" concerns:
options: Deciding the method of production to be used
Deciding which goods and services, and in what quantities, should be produced with scarce resources
Deciding who receives the goods produced
Deciding the currency to be used in exchange
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Deciding which goods and services, and in what quantities, should be produced with scarce resources

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: The basic economic problem of "how to produce" is resolved differently across economic systems mainly through:
options: The size of a country's population
The location of the capital city
The choice of production technique, whether determined by market forces or by state planning
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: The choice of production technique, whether determined by market forces or by state planning

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: The economic problem of "for whom to produce" deals with:
options: Which raw materials are used in production
How goods and services are distributed among members of society
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: How goods and services are distributed among members of society

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: Which of the following best distinguishes socialism from communism?
options: They are identical systems with no differences
Communism is always a capitalist system
Socialism generally allows for some state control with limited private property, while pure communism envisages a classless society with no private property at all
Socialism has no role for government at all
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Socialism generally allows for some state control with limited private property, while pure communism envisages a classless society with no private property at all

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: In a free market (capitalist) economy, prices of goods are mainly determined by:
options: The interaction of demand and supply
Traditional rules passed down by elders
The size of the national budget
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: The interaction of demand and supply

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: In a socialist economy, decisions about production and resource allocation are typically made by:
options: A central planning authority acting on behalf of the state
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: A central planning authority acting on behalf of the state

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: The profit motive, which drives individuals to maximise gain, is most strongly associated with which economic system?
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Capitalism

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: Public corporations such as state-owned electricity or water boards operating alongside private businesses are most characteristic of a:
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Mixed economy

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: "Laissez-faire" is a term closely associated with which economic system?
options: Capitalism, because it implies minimal government interference in the economy
Socialism, because government controls all production
Mixed economy, because government and private firms are equal partners
Communism, because there is no private ownership
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Capitalism, because it implies minimal government interference in the economy

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: "Consumer sovereignty", the idea that consumers' spending decisions determine what is produced, is a key feature of:
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: A capitalist market economy

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: State ownership of the major means of production, such as factories, land, and financial institutions, is a defining feature of:
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Socialism

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: A "command economy" is another name closely associated with:
options: Socialism, since the state directs economic activity
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Socialism, since the state directs economic activity

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: Which economic system relies most heavily on the price mechanism to solve the problem of "what to produce"?
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Capitalism

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.text: Which economic system is most often criticised for producing high levels of unemployment and income inequality due to limited government intervention?
Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Capitalism

Types and Basic Features of Economic Sys.correct_answer: Socialism

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: If total utility from 3 units is 40 utils and from 4 units is 46 utils, the marginal utility of the 4th unit is
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: 6 utils

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: One major implication of the consumer equilibrium condition is that the consumer's
options: satisfaction is maximised given income and prices
demand for all goods becomes equal
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: satisfaction is maximised given income and prices

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: Consumer surplus refers to the
options: amount a consumer saves by buying on credit
difference between what a consumer is willing to pay and what is actually paid
total income left after purchasing all goods
extra tax paid on a commodity
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: difference between what a consumer is willing to pay and what is actually paid

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: Consumer surplus arises largely because of the
options: equality of price and total utility
diminishing nature of marginal utility as more units are consumed
rising nature of marginal utility as more units are consumed
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: diminishing nature of marginal utility as more units are consumed

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: As a consumer takes successive units of a commodity within a given period, marginal utility generally tends to
options: rise then fall sharply to zero at once
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: decrease

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: Which of the following is often cited as an exception to the law of diminishing marginal utility?
options: collecting rare items such as coins or stamps
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: collecting rare items such as coins or stamps

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: The principle guiding a rational consumer allocating income among several goods is known as the law of
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: equi-marginal utility

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: If the marginal utility per naira spent on good X exceeds that on good Y, a rational consumer should
options: buy more of Y and less of X
buy more of X and less of Y
buy equal amounts of X and Y immediately
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: buy more of X and less of Y

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: A consumer who keeps consuming a good even after reaching the point of maximum total utility will experience
options: a fall in total utility as marginal utility turns negative
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: a fall in total utility as marginal utility turns negative

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: A basic assumption of the cardinalist theory of consumer behaviour is that
options: utility is a purely measurable, additive quantity
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: utility is a purely measurable, additive quantity

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: Which of the following would NOT normally be considered a direct determinant of the utility a consumer derives from a good?
options: the number of shareholders in the producing firm
the quantity of the good already consumed
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: the number of shareholders in the producing firm

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: The point at which marginal utility becomes zero is also called the point of
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: satiety (saturation)

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: The theory of consumer behaviour is mainly used by economists to explain
options: how wages are determined in the labour market
why the demand curve for a normal good slopes downward
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: why the demand curve for a normal good slopes downward

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: The downward slope of an individual's demand curve for a commodity is closely linked to the
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: law of diminishing marginal utility

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: Compared with later units, the first unit of a commodity consumed within a period typically yields
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: the highest marginal utility

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: Utility is described as subjective mainly because it
options: is the same for every consumer
varies from one consumer to another and from time to time
can be traded in the market like a commodity
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: varies from one consumer to another and from time to time

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: At consumer equilibrium involving many goods, a rational consumer's entire income is
options: spent entirely on the cheapest good only
spent entirely on the most expensive good only
spent such that the marginal utility per naira is equalised across all goods bought
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: spent such that the marginal utility per naira is equalised across all goods bought

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: If a consumer's income increases while prices remain unchanged, to reach a new equilibrium the consumer will typically
options: buy more of normal goods until marginal utilities per naira are again equalised
keep spending exactly the same amount as before
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: buy more of normal goods until marginal utilities per naira are again equalised

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: The condition for consumer equilibrium can be summarised as spending the whole budget so that
options: marginal utility of each good is the same in absolute terms
the ratio of marginal utility to price is equal for every good purchased
total utility of every good purchased is equal
average utility of every good purchased is equal
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: the ratio of marginal utility to price is equal for every good purchased

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: A student records the total utility from eating oranges as: 1st orange = 10 utils, 2nd = 18 utils, 3rd = 24 utils, 4th = 24 utils. The marginal utility of the 4th orange is
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: 0 utils

Theory of Consumer Behaviour.text: The term used to describe the satisfaction a consumer derives from consuming goods and services is
Theory of Consumer Behaviour.correct_answer: utility

Theory of Price Determination.text: In economics, a market is best defined as
options: any arrangement that brings buyers and sellers together to exchange goods and services
a physical building where goods are displayed for sale
a place where only farm produce is sold
a government agency that fixes prices
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: any arrangement that brings buyers and sellers together to exchange goods and services

Theory of Price Determination.text: Which of the following is NOT a necessary feature of a market?
options: a fixed physical location in all cases
a commodity or service to be exchanged
a means of communication between buyers and sellers
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: a fixed physical location in all cases

Theory of Price Determination.text: The equilibrium price of a commodity is the price at which
options: government fixes the price by law
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied

Theory of Price Determination.text: Equilibrium price is determined in a free market mainly through the
options: interaction of the forces of demand and supply
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: interaction of the forces of demand and supply

Theory of Price Determination.text: On a demand and supply diagram, the equilibrium price is found
options: at the intersection of the demand and supply curves
where the demand curve cuts the vertical axis
above the point where demand and supply curves intersect
where the supply curve cuts the horizontal axis
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: at the intersection of the demand and supply curves

Theory of Price Determination.text: If, at a given price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, there is a
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: shortage

Theory of Price Determination.text: If, at a given price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, there is a
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: surplus

Theory of Price Determination.text: When there is a shortage of a commodity at the prevailing price in a free market, price will tend to
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: rise until equilibrium is restored

Theory of Price Determination.text: When there is a surplus of a commodity at the prevailing price in a free market, price will tend to
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: fall until equilibrium is restored

Theory of Price Determination.text: A free (uncontrolled) market is one in which
options: prices are determined solely by the forces of demand and supply without government interference
only cooperative societies are allowed to trade
trade is banned to prevent price changes
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: prices are determined solely by the forces of demand and supply without government interference

Theory of Price Determination.text: A controlled (regulated) market is one in which
options: prices are left entirely to demand and supply
goods are exchanged only by barter
government or an authority intervenes to influence or fix prices
there are no buyers, only sellers
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: government or an authority intervenes to influence or fix prices

Theory of Price Determination.text: A price ceiling (maximum price) is a government-imposed price that is set
options: above the equilibrium price to protect producers
below the equilibrium price to protect consumers
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: below the equilibrium price to protect consumers

Theory of Price Determination.text: A price floor (minimum price) is a government-imposed price that is set
options: above the equilibrium price to protect producers
below the equilibrium price to protect consumers
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: above the equilibrium price to protect producers

Theory of Price Determination.text: A maximum price policy, if set below equilibrium, is likely to create
options: a persistent surplus of the commodity
a persistent shortage of the commodity
an immediate fall in demand to zero
no effect on the market at all
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: a persistent shortage of the commodity

Theory of Price Determination.text: A minimum price policy, if set above equilibrium, is likely to create
options: a persistent shortage of the commodity
an immediate fall in supply to zero
a persistent surplus of the commodity
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: a persistent surplus of the commodity

Theory of Price Determination.text: A common consequence of an effective price ceiling on an essential commodity is the emergence of a
options: fall in the price below the ceiling
reduction in consumer demand for the commodity
black market where the commodity is sold above the legal price
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: black market where the commodity is sold above the legal price

Theory of Price Determination.text: Governments often set a minimum price (price floor) for agricultural produce mainly in order to
options: guarantee farmers a fair and stable income
increase the quantity demanded by consumers
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: guarantee farmers a fair and stable income

Theory of Price Determination.text: Governments often impose a maximum price on essential goods mainly to
options: make the goods affordable to low-income consumers
reduce the supply of the goods
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: make the goods affordable to low-income consumers

Theory of Price Determination.text: In a free market, if demand for a commodity increases while supply remains unchanged, equilibrium price will tend to
options: fall and equilibrium quantity will fall
remain the same while quantity falls
rise and equilibrium quantity will rise
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: rise and equilibrium quantity will rise

Theory of Price Determination.text: In a free market, if supply of a commodity increases while demand remains unchanged, equilibrium price will tend to
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: fall while equilibrium quantity rises

Theory of Price Determination.text: The process by which price rises when there is a shortage and falls when there is a surplus, moving the market toward equilibrium, is often called the
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: market mechanism (price mechanism)

Theory of Price Determination.text: Which of the following best describes a black market?
options: an official government store selling controlled goods
an illegal market where goods are sold above the officially fixed price
a market that operates only at night
a market for used goods only
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: an illegal market where goods are sold above the officially fixed price

Theory of Price Determination.text: One likely effect of a minimum price policy that creates a persistent surplus is that the government may need to
options: reduce the price further below equilibrium
buy up and store the surplus produce
ban the sale of the commodity entirely
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: buy up and store the surplus produce

Theory of Price Determination.text: A market where the identity of the market is not tied to a physical location, such as an online marketplace or a stock exchange linked by telephone and internet, illustrates that a market requires
options: the presence of a middleman only
communication between buyers and sellers rather than a fixed location
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: communication between buyers and sellers rather than a fixed location

Theory of Price Determination.text: Which of the following is an example of a controlled market situation?
options: government fixing the price of petroleum products
a village market where prices change freely with demand and supply
a farmer selling produce at whatever price a buyer offers
an auction where the highest bidder wins
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: government fixing the price of petroleum products

Theory of Price Determination.text: At the equilibrium price, the market is said to be cleared because
options: there is neither a shortage nor a surplus of the commodity
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: there is neither a shortage nor a surplus of the commodity

Theory of Price Determination.text: If government sets a price ceiling exactly at the free-market equilibrium price, the immediate effect on quantity demanded and supplied will most likely be
options: little or no change, since the ceiling equals equilibrium
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: little or no change, since the ceiling equals equilibrium

Theory of Price Determination.text: One disadvantage of a price ceiling below equilibrium is that it may lead to
options: an automatic rise in supply to match demand
a fall in consumer demand to zero
reduced incentive for producers to supply the commodity, worsening shortages
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: reduced incentive for producers to supply the commodity, worsening shortages

Theory of Price Determination.text: One disadvantage of a price floor above equilibrium for consumers is that it
options: makes the commodity more expensive than the free-market price
lowers the price they must pay
eliminates the commodity from the market entirely
guarantees them unlimited supply at no cost
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: makes the commodity more expensive than the free-market price

Theory of Price Determination.text: Rationing by coupons is sometimes introduced by government alongside a price ceiling mainly to
options: increase the price of the commodity
allocate a scarce commodity fairly among consumers
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: allocate a scarce commodity fairly among consumers

Theory of Price Determination.text: Which of the following is a typical example of a minimum wage policy?
options: government fixing the highest price consumers may pay for bread
a firm voluntarily reducing wages during a recession
government fixing the lowest price a fixed quantity of labour may legally be paid
workers agreeing among themselves to reduce their pay
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: government fixing the lowest price a fixed quantity of labour may legally be paid

Theory of Price Determination.text: In price theory, the term "excess demand" at a given price is another way of describing a
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: shortage

Theory of Price Determination.text: In price theory, the term "excess supply" at a given price is another way of describing a
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: surplus

Theory of Price Determination.text: Compared with a free market, one advantage of a controlled market is that it can
options: protect vulnerable consumers or producers from extreme price movements
always increase efficiency in resource allocation
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: protect vulnerable consumers or producers from extreme price movements

Theory of Price Determination.text: Compared with a controlled market, one advantage often claimed for a free market is that it
options: always guarantees equal incomes for everyone
allows prices to allocate resources efficiently based on demand and supply signals
guarantees there will never be a surplus or shortage
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: allows prices to allocate resources efficiently based on demand and supply signals

Theory of Price Determination.text: If the government imposes a support (minimum) price on maize above equilibrium and buys the resulting surplus, this policy is generally intended to benefit
options: maize farmers, by guaranteeing a higher and more stable price
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: maize farmers, by guaranteeing a higher and more stable price

Theory of Price Determination.text: A sudden increase in supply of tomatoes during a bumper harvest, with demand unchanged, will most likely cause
options: the equilibrium price to fall and quantity traded to rise
both price and quantity to fall
no change in price or quantity
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: the equilibrium price to fall and quantity traded to rise

Theory of Price Determination.text: A sudden fall in the supply of rice due to a poor harvest, with demand unchanged, will most likely cause
options: the equilibrium price to fall and quantity traded to rise
the equilibrium price to rise and quantity traded to fall
both price and quantity to rise
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: the equilibrium price to rise and quantity traded to fall

Theory of Price Determination.text: Which market situation would MOST likely encourage hoarding and the growth of a black market?
options: a minimum price set below equilibrium
a free market with no price controls
a maximum price set well below equilibrium for a scarce essential good
equilibrium price determined purely by demand and supply
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: a maximum price set well below equilibrium for a scarce essential good

Theory of Price Determination.text: The theory of price determination is primarily concerned with explaining how
options: government fixes all prices in the economy
the price and quantity of a commodity are set through the interaction of demand and supply
Theory of Price Determination.correct_answer: the price and quantity of a commodity are set through the interaction of demand and supply

Theory of Production.text: Division of labour refers to the
options: breaking down of a production process into separate tasks performed by different workers
equal sharing of profits among workers
Theory of Production.correct_answer: breaking down of a production process into separate tasks performed by different workers

Theory of Production.text: Specialisation in production occurs when a worker, firm, or region
options: produces a wide variety of goods to be self-sufficient
concentrates on producing a particular good, service, or task in which it is most efficient
produces only for its own consumption
Theory of Production.correct_answer: concentrates on producing a particular good, service, or task in which it is most efficient

Theory of Production.text: Which of the following is a recognised advantage of division of labour?
options: greater risk of unemployment during economic booms
reduced total output of the economy
increased worker skill and speed from repeating the same task
elimination of the need for machinery
Theory of Production.correct_answer: increased worker skill and speed from repeating the same task

Theory of Production.text: One major disadvantage of division of labour is that it can lead to
options: greater flexibility of workers across different jobs
monotony and boredom for workers performing repetitive tasks
Theory of Production.correct_answer: monotony and boredom for workers performing repetitive tasks

Theory of Production.text: A key disadvantage of extreme division of labour on a production line is that
options: workers become highly dependent on one another, so a breakdown in one stage can halt the whole process
it increases the skill required of each worker in all areas of production
it eliminates the need for cooperation between workers
Theory of Production.correct_answer: workers become highly dependent on one another, so a breakdown in one stage can halt the whole process

Theory of Production.text: Division of labour typically leads to increased productivity mainly because it
options: requires every worker to learn every task
allows workers to specialise and become more skilled and efficient at specific tasks
reduces the total number of goods produced
Theory of Production.correct_answer: allows workers to specialise and become more skilled and efficient at specific tasks

Theory of Production.text: Economies of scale refer to the
options: rise in average cost of production as a firm expands its output
fall in total revenue as output increases
reduction in average cost of production as a firm increases its scale of output
increase in the number of firms in an industry
Theory of Production.correct_answer: reduction in average cost of production as a firm increases its scale of output

Theory of Production.text: Internal economies of scale are cost advantages that arise
options: from the growth of the whole industry, benefiting all firms in it
purely by chance and cannot be explained
only when government grants a subsidy
within a single firm as a result of its own growth in size
Theory of Production.correct_answer: within a single firm as a result of its own growth in size

Theory of Production.text: External economies of scale are cost advantages that a firm enjoys as a result of
options: the growth of the whole industry or locality in which it operates
Theory of Production.correct_answer: the growth of the whole industry or locality in which it operates

Theory of Production.text: Which of the following is an example of an internal economy of scale?
options: the development of a skilled labour pool in an industrial area
bulk-buying of raw materials at discounted prices by a large firm
improved transport and infrastructure built for a whole industrial zone
the establishment of specialised suppliers serving many firms in an area
Theory of Production.correct_answer: bulk-buying of raw materials at discounted prices by a large firm

Theory of Production.text: Which of the following is an example of an external economy of scale?
options: a large firm's ability to employ specialist managers
a firm's use of large-scale, more efficient machinery
the growth of a pool of skilled labour in an area due to the concentration of many firms in the same industry
a firm spreading its fixed costs over a larger output
Theory of Production.correct_answer: the growth of a pool of skilled labour in an area due to the concentration of many firms in the same industry

Theory of Production.text: Technical economies of scale arise mainly because larger firms can
options: borrow money at higher interest rates
reduce the quality of their products
use large, specialised, and more efficient machinery and production methods
Theory of Production.correct_answer: use large, specialised, and more efficient machinery and production methods

Theory of Production.text: Financial economies of scale refer to the advantage large firms have in
options: obtaining loans and credit more easily and at lower interest rates than small firms
avoiding the need for any capital
paying higher prices for raw materials
reducing the size of their workforce
Theory of Production.correct_answer: obtaining loans and credit more easily and at lower interest rates than small firms

Theory of Production.text: Managerial economies of scale occur when a large firm is able to
options: eliminate the need for any management structure
employ specialist managers and departments, improving efficiency
reduce output to a single unit
Theory of Production.correct_answer: employ specialist managers and departments, improving efficiency

Theory of Production.text: Diseconomies of scale occur when a firm expands beyond its optimum size and
options: average cost of production begins to fall further
average cost of production begins to rise due to inefficiencies such as poor coordination
the firm automatically becomes more profitable
Theory of Production.correct_answer: average cost of production begins to rise due to inefficiencies such as poor coordination

Theory of Production.text: A common cause of internal diseconomies of scale in a very large firm is
options: lower average costs from bulk buying
difficulties of coordination and control as the organisation becomes too large and complex
Theory of Production.correct_answer: difficulties of coordination and control as the organisation becomes too large and complex

Theory of Production.text: Total product refers to the
options: total quantity of output produced by a given combination of factors of production
output produced by the last unit of a variable factor employed
total output divided by the number of units of the variable factor employed
cost incurred in producing one unit of output
Theory of Production.correct_answer: total quantity of output produced by a given combination of factors of production

Theory of Production.text: Average product is calculated as
options: total product divided by the quantity of the variable factor employed
change in total product divided by change in fixed factor
marginal product divided by total product
Theory of Production.correct_answer: total product divided by the quantity of the variable factor employed

Theory of Production.text: Marginal product refers to the
options: total output produced by all units of the variable factor
average output produced per unit of the variable factor
additional output produced by employing one more unit of the variable factor
output produced when no variable factor is employed
Theory of Production.correct_answer: additional output produced by employing one more unit of the variable factor

Theory of Production.text: The law of variable proportions (law of diminishing returns) states that as more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor, output will
options: increase at a constant rate forever
always fall from the very first unit
remain unchanged regardless of the units added
eventually increase at a diminishing rate and marginal product will fall
Theory of Production.correct_answer: eventually increase at a diminishing rate and marginal product will fall

Theory of Production.text: The law of variable proportions applies specifically in the
options: short run, when at least one factor of production is fixed
long run, when all factors of production are variable
Theory of Production.correct_answer: short run, when at least one factor of production is fixed

Theory of Production.text: In the first stage of the law of variable proportions, as more units of the variable factor are added, total product
options: increases at an increasing rate and marginal product rises
increases at a decreasing rate only
Theory of Production.correct_answer: increases at an increasing rate and marginal product rises

Theory of Production.text: In the second stage of the law of variable proportions, total product continues to rise but
options: marginal product is positive but falling
total product also begins to fall
Theory of Production.correct_answer: marginal product is positive but falling

Theory of Production.text: In the third stage of the law of variable proportions, total product begins to fall because
options: fixed factors are removed from production
Theory of Production.correct_answer: marginal product becomes negative

Theory of Production.text: A rational producer would normally choose to operate in the stage of production where
options: average product is rising and marginal product is falling but still positive
no variable factor is employed at all
Theory of Production.correct_answer: average product is rising and marginal product is falling but still positive

Theory of Production.text: Total product is at its maximum when
options: marginal product is at its highest positive value
Theory of Production.correct_answer: marginal product is zero

Theory of Production.text: A key assumption of the law of variable proportions is that
options: all factors of production are variable
technology remains unchanged while the variable factor is increased
output prices are fixed by the government
Theory of Production.correct_answer: technology remains unchanged while the variable factor is increased

Theory of Production.text: A farmer keeps adding more labourers to a fixed plot of land. Beyond a certain point, output per additional labourer begins to fall. This illustrates
options: the law of variable proportions (diminishing returns)
Theory of Production.correct_answer: the law of variable proportions (diminishing returns)

Theory of Production.text: If total product is 100 units from 5 workers and 108 units from 6 workers, the marginal product of the 6th worker is
Theory of Production.correct_answer: 8 units

Theory of Production.text: If total product from 4 workers is 80 units, the average product per worker is
Theory of Production.correct_answer: 20 units

Theory of Production.text: One key advantage of division of labour to an economy as a whole is that it tends to
options: eliminate the need for trade between regions
increase overall productivity and total output
make workers less skilled over time
Theory of Production.correct_answer: increase overall productivity and total output

Theory of Production.text: Excessive division of labour on an assembly line may reduce job satisfaction mainly because workers
options: earn much higher wages as a result
gain a wide variety of skills
perform only a small, repetitive part of the whole production process
Theory of Production.correct_answer: perform only a small, repetitive part of the whole production process

Theory of Production.text: The optimum size of a firm is generally the size at which
options: average cost of production is at its lowest
total cost of production is highest
the firm produces the smallest possible output
Theory of Production.correct_answer: average cost of production is at its lowest

Theory of Production.text: Which of the following best illustrates an external diseconomy of scale affecting firms in a rapidly growing industrial area?
options: traffic congestion and higher costs for all firms as the industrial area becomes overcrowded
a single firm hiring a specialist accountant
a single firm negotiating a bulk discount on raw materials
Theory of Production.correct_answer: traffic congestion and higher costs for all firms as the industrial area becomes overcrowded

Theory of Production.text: Marketing economies of scale allow large firms to reduce average costs mainly by
options: increasing the price of raw materials
reducing the size of their sales force to zero
buying inputs and advertising in bulk at lower unit cost
Theory of Production.correct_answer: buying inputs and advertising in bulk at lower unit cost

Theory of Production.text: Risk-bearing economies of scale refer to the ability of large firms to
options: reduce the number of customers they serve
spread risk by diversifying into several products or markets
Theory of Production.correct_answer: spread risk by diversifying into several products or markets

Theory of Production.text: Which of the following statements about the law of variable proportions is TRUE?
options: it explains why, in the short run, adding more of a variable factor to a fixed factor eventually yields diminishing extra output
it applies only when all factors, including the fixed factor, are increased simultaneously
it guarantees that output will rise indefinitely as more variable factor is added
it is unrelated to the concept of marginal product
Theory of Production.correct_answer: it explains why, in the short run, adding more of a variable factor to a fixed factor eventually yields diminishing extra output

Theory of Production.text: As long as marginal product is greater than average product, average product will be
Theory of Production.correct_answer: rising

Theory of Production.text: As soon as marginal product falls below average product, average product will begin to
Theory of Production.correct_answer: fall

Theory of Production.text: Adam Smith's classic example of division of labour, often cited in economics, involved the manufacture of
Theory of Production.correct_answer: pins in a pin factory

Theory of Cost and Revenue.text: The cost that does not vary with the level of output in the short run is known as ____.
Which of the following is an example of variable cost to a bakery?
Total cost (TC) is best defined as ____.
options: The sum of fixed cost and variable cost
Theory of Cost and Revenue.correct_answer: The sum of fixed cost and variable cost

Theory of Cost and Revenue.text: Average cost (AC) is obtained by ____.
options: subtracting fixed cost from total cost
dividing total cost by total output
Theory of Cost and Revenue.correct_answer: dividing total cost by total output

Theory of Cost and Revenue.text: Marginal cost is defined as ____.
options: the cost of producing the first unit of output
total cost divided by total output
the sum of all fixed costs
the addition to total cost from producing one more unit of output
Theory of Cost and Revenue.correct_answer: the addition to total cost from producing one more unit of output

Theory of Cost and Revenue.text: A firm's fixed cost is ₦20,000 and its total variable cost for producing 100 units is ₦30,000. What is the total cost?
Using the data in question 6, what is the average cost per unit?
Which cost remains unchanged even when a firm's output is zero?
If the total cost of producing 10 units is ₦5,000 and the total cost of producing 11 units is ₦5,400, what is the marginal cost of the 11th unit?
Average fixed cost (AFC) continuously falls as output increases because ____.
options: fixed cost is spread over a larger output
variable cost rises faster than output
Theory of Cost and Revenue.correct_answer: fixed cost is spread over a larger output

Theory of Cost and Revenue.text: Which of the following best represents a fixed cost for a factory?
options: Wages of casual labourers paid per unit produced
Cost of electricity used in production
Annual rent on the factory building
Theory of Cost and Revenue.correct_answer: Annual rent on the factory building

Theory of Cost and Revenue.text: A firm produces 50 units at a total variable cost of ₦15,000. What is the average variable cost?
The concept of cost that includes both explicit and implicit costs is used mainly by ____.
Explicit costs are also known as ____.
Implicit cost refers to ____.
options: the estimated value of self-owned resources used in production
actual cash payment made by a firm
the cost of raw materials purchased
Theory of Cost and Revenue.correct_answer: the estimated value of self-owned resources used in production

Theory of Cost and Revenue.text: Normal profit is best described as ____.
options: profit above what is needed to keep a firm in business
the minimum reward necessary to keep an entrepreneur in a particular line of business
Theory of Cost and Revenue.correct_answer: the minimum reward necessary to keep an entrepreneur in a particular line of business

Theory of Cost and Revenue.text: An accountant, unlike an economist, when calculating profit typically ____.
If a firm's total revenue equals its total cost, including implicit costs, the firm is said to be earning ____.
The salary an entrepreneur forgoes by running her own business instead of working for another firm is an example of ____.
Economic (supernormal) profit exists when ____.
options: total revenue is less than total cost
total revenue equals explicit cost only
total revenue exceeds total cost, including implicit costs
Theory of Cost and Revenue.correct_answer: total revenue exceeds total cost, including implicit costs

Theory of Cost and Revenue.text: Which of these is NOT an explicit cost?

Market Structures.text: Which of the following is a barrier to entry associated with monopoly?

Market Structures.text: Under perfect competition, price is determined by ____.

the largest firm in the industry

firms cannot enter or exit freely
many firms selling slightly differentiated products

Market Structures.text: Which of the following best describes an oligopoly?

One firm controlling the entire market
A few dominant firms controlling a large share of the market
Free entry with no barriers at all

Market Structures.text: Non-price competition, such as advertising and branding, is most associated with ____.

there is perfect information among buyers

Market Structures.text: The kinked demand curve theory is used to explain price ____ under oligopoly.

Market Structures.text: Under perfect competition, in the short run a firm will shut down production if price falls below ____.

Market Structures.text: Which of these is NOT a characteristic of a monopoly market?

Market Structures.text: In monopolistic competition, firms compete mainly through ____.

a firm operating under perfect competition

Market Structures.text: Which of the following is a key difference between perfect competition and monopoly?

Market Structures.text: A market with only two sellers is known as ____.

Market Structures.text: One necessary condition for price discrimination to be effective is that ____.

all consumers must have identical incomes
products must be homogeneous across all firms in the industry
Market Structures.correct_answer: the seller must be able to prevent resale between the two markets

the firm must operate under perfect competition
there must be completely free entry into the industry
government must fix a single price for all markets

Market Structures.text: Charging students a lower cinema ticket price than adults for the same show is an example of ____.
Market Structures.correct_answer: price discrimination

Market Structures.text: First-degree price discrimination involves ____.

charging a uniform price based on quantity blocks only

Market Structures.text: Second-degree price discrimination involves ____.

charging different prices for different blocks/quantities of the same good
charging based on the time of day only, with no other basis

Market Structures.text: Third-degree price discrimination involves ____.

offering the same price to all markets
dividing buyers into separate groups/markets and charging each group a different price

Market Structures.text: An example of third-degree price discrimination is ____.

a firm charging a single uniform national price
a firm giving the same discount to everyone regardless of group

Market Structures.text: Price discrimination is most likely to be practiced by ____.

a firm producing homogeneous goods with no market power

Market Structures.text: One reason a monopolist practices price discrimination is to ____.

Market Structures.correct_answer: increase total revenue and profit by exploiting different elasticities of demand

Market Structures.text: Which of the following is required for a market to be effectively separated for price discrimination?

Consumers in different markets must not be able to easily transfer the product between markets

Market Structures.text: Airlines charging business travellers more than tourists for similar seats is an example of ____.

Market Structures.text: A major disadvantage of price discrimination to consumers in the higher-priced market is that ____.
